title: Abortion Access in PA
raw_text:
This page will provide you with some information about the state of abortion access in Pennsylvania.
What does the reversal of Roe v. Wade mean?
The Supreme Court has overturned Roe v Wade, which means that there is no constitutional right to an abortion. This puts the decision of abortion in the hands of the states. Currently, abortion is STILL LEGAL in Pennsylvania. It will be up to the voters to decide which leaders are elected to represent their rights.
Is abortion legal in Pennsylvania?
Yes, abortion is still legal in Pennsylvania. Current law states that abortion is accessible, however, there are several restrictions to abortion access:
Prohibited at 24 weeks gestational age (from last menstrual period).
Prohibits the use of state and federal Medical Assistance (MA) Funds for abortion services, unless the pregnancy is a result of reported rape or incest, or abortion is necessary to avert the death of the pregnant person.
Mandated counseling from abortion provider that includes information designed to discourage the patient from having an abortion and 24 hour wait before getting an abortion. This waiting period can be waived if health is at risk because of the pregnancy.
If under the age of 18, a parent or guardian must give permission to get an abortion or request a judicial bypass to waive the requirement for parental involvement.
Requiring a signed notice under penalty from a married woman that she has notified her spouse she is about to undergo an abortion (with exceptions for medical emergencies or if the pregnancy resulted from spousal sexual assault).
Where can I get an abortion?
Abortion access should come from a reputable organization.   Planned Parenthood has been a leading provider of reproductive health services in Reading for years.
1920 Kutztown Rd. Reading PA 19604   phone: 610-376-8061
Book your appt online at Birth Control, STD Testing & Abortion – Reading, PA (plannedparenthood.org)
Be wary of Crisis Pregnancy Centers. These are fake clinics that use deceptive tactics to coerce women into continuing their pregnancy.   They do not offer or refer to abortion providers.
What does the reversal of Roe v. Wade mean?
If the Supreme Court decides to overturn Roe v. Wade, there would be no constitutional right to an abortion, and the authority over abortion law goes to the individual states.
Does pa have trigger laws?
You may have heard the term “trigger law” or “trigger ban.”  These are bans that will take effect immediately after Roe v Wade is overturned.
Pennsylvania does not have a “trigger law” in place.
Has legislation been introduced to ban or restrict abortion in Pennsylvania?
Yes, multiple bills have been introduced that would ban or restrict abortion access.
S.B. 378 (Mastriano)
H.B. 904 (Borowicz)
– Would prohibit the abortion of a fetus if a heartbeat is detected, changing current statutory requirements for an abortion from 24 weeks to 6 weeks gestation. If no fetal heartbeat is detected, an abortion may only be performed if a physician determines an abortion is necessary.
Status
–
B. 378 was referred to the Senate Health and Human Services Committee on March 10, 2021.
Status
– H.B. 904 received first consideration on the House Floor on May 25, 2021. The bill was tabled for a second time in the House on September 20, 2021.
S.B. 956 (J.Ward)
H.B. 2252 (Oberlander)
– Would amend the Pennsylvania Constitution to declare there is no right to an abortion or funding for an abortion.
Status
– On January 25, 2022, S.B. 956 was reported as committed by the Senate Health and Human Services Committee and received first consideration on the Senate Floor. The bill was laid on the table on April 12, 2022.
Status
– H.B. 2252 was referred to the House Health Committee on January 20, 2022.
S.B. 152 (J.Ward)
– Would prohibit the Department of Health from entering into contracts with or making grants to entities that perform abortions that do not qualify for federal matching funds through Medicaid or that maintain or operate facilities where such abortions are performed, except as required by federal law when such services are provided by Medicaid and by a qualified provider approved by the Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services.
Status
– S.B. 152 was reported as committed by the Senate Health and Human Services Committee and received first consideration on the Senate Floor on January 25, 2022. The bill was removed from the table on April 12, 2022.
S.B. 289 (O’Neal)
–
Would require abortion facilities to publicly post and update inspection information online and provide inspection information to individuals upon request at no cost. Plans of correction must be posted on a facility’s public website within 30 days of receiving notice of a violation or sooner, as directed by the Department of Health.  Facilities must ensure the identities of their patients remain confidential when posting such information.
Status
– H.B. 289 was referred to the House Health Committee on January 27, 2021.
S.B. 1500 (Klunk)
– Would prohibit an abortion for the reason of a prenatal diagnosis of Down Syndrome. The bill would change the penalty of a physician that performs an abortion for this reason, providing for that physician’s medical and surgical licenses to be revoked instead of allowing for suspension or revocation.  A person receiving or attempting to receive an abortion due to the fetus’ sex or prenatal diagnosis of Down Syndrome shall not be guilty of committing, attempting to commit, conspiring to commit or being complicit in committing a prohibited abortion.  A written statement must be provided to the Department of Health by the physician performing the abortion indicating the person did not seek an abortion because of the sex of the fetus or a prenatal diagnosis, test result or indication of Down Syndrome in the fetus.
Status
– H.B. 1500 passed the House on third consideration on June 8, 2021 by a vote of 120:83. The bill is currently in the Senate, where it received first consideration on June 21, 2021.
The bill was removed from the table for a third time on April 4, 2022.
S.B. 1872 (Bonner)
– Would require the administration of pain medication to a fetus aborted at more than 12 weeks gestation unless the physician has prior knowledge of the pregnant person’s adverse reaction to pain relief medication or there is insufficient time to administer medication prior to the abortion due to a medical emergency.
Status
– H.B. 1872 was referred to the House Health Committee on September 16, 2021.
S.B. 21 (Martin)
– Would prohibit the abortion of a fetus based on the sex of the fetus and/or a prenatal diagnosis or belief that the fetus has Down Syndrome.
Status
– S.B. 21 was referred to the Senate Health and Human Services Committee
on January 20, 2021.
Other facts about abortion.
1 in 4 women will have had an abortion by the time they turn 45 years old.
Abortion is a safe procedure with dramatically less health risks than childbirth.
95% of women who had abortions continued to feel confident about their decision.
In 2020, there were 32,123 abortions performed in Pennsylvania.
Abortion by race and age groups
What is a medication abortion?
Medication abortion is a non-surgical abortion where the patient ends their pregnancy by taking a pill or series of pills.
Mifepristone, approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2000, is used with another medication called misoprostol to end early pregnancy. Mifepristone is well established in medical literature as a safe alternative to surgical abortion.
In 2019, 45% of all abortions provided in Pennsylvania were medical abortions.
How does it work?
The regimen of pills can be taken safely at home, a method increasingly used around the world.
The protocol approved for use in the United States includes two medications. The first one, mifepristone, blocks a hormone called progesterone that is necessary for a pregnancy to continue. The second, misoprostol, brings on uterine contractions.
The combination of these pills causes a complete abortion in more than 99 percent of patients.
What are some common barriers to care?
Although medication abortion is
safe
and
effective
, many women have difficulties accessing care. Barriers to safe legal abortion include
Money
Travel logistics
Limited clinics
State restrictions
These factors all result in delayed care, negative mental health consequences, and the consideration of unsafe methods to end a pregnancy. Black and Brown communities and low-income earners are disproportionately impacted.
How can I become involved?
There are a lot of ways to be involved in the fight for reproductive justice.
Volunteer with Planned Parenthood. You can choose how you want to help, whenever you have time.  Whether it’s attending a rally, being a patient escort, or donating to the cause.  Every action is appreciated.
Be vocal. Abortion will lose its stigma when people realize that it’s common.  If you have a story, share it.

About the Program
The
Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
helps families living on low incomes pay their heating bills in the form of a cash grant. Households in immediate danger of being without heat can also qualify for crisis grants
.
The cash grant is a one-time payment sent directly to the utility company/fuel provider to be credited on your bill. You can receive from $200 to $1,000 based on your household size, income, and fuel type.  Remember: This is a grant and does not have to be repaid.

Our Mission
The Pennsylvania Women’s Health Caucus is a bipartisan, bicameral caucus of legislators partnering with advocacy groups to advance legislation and policies that promote equity and protect the health and wellbeing of women, gender expansive people, and families in Pennsylvania. As a caucus, we recognize the intersectionality of social issues that support physical and mental health. We are committed to closing existing disparities and removing barriers Pennsylvanians of all backgrounds face when seeking healthcare and systems of support. Integral to our mission is the belief that all Pennsylvanians have the right to make private, personal medical decisions.

title: Senate Democratic Policy Committee Hearing on Addressing Today’s Challenges in Agriculture and Farming
raw_text:
Senate Democratic Policy Committee Hearing on Addressing Today’s Challenges in Agriculture and Farming
October 6, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA − October 6, 2026 −
Senate Democratic Policy Committee Chair Nick Miller (D-14) hosted a policy hearing on addressing today’s challenges in agriculture and farming, alongside co-hosts Senator Judy Schwank (D-11) and Senator James Malone (D-36). This hearing examined current state-level tools and supports while identifying forward‑looking policy solutions. As stakeholders face challenges like workforce impacts, disease management, severe weather, and rising input costs, the Committee heard expert testimony from Secretary Redding and other industry leaders.
“Pennsylvania farmers are facing growing challenges, from rising costs and unpredictable weather to a shrinking pipeline of young farmers,” said
Senator Nick Miller
. “We must act now to ensure agriculture remains a cornerstone of our Commonwealth. Today’s hearing highlighted important solutions we can consider to provide farmers with the resources they need, support the next generation, and protect Pennsylvania’s agricultural heritage.”
“Today’s hearing was a valuable opportunity to get an understand of what this past year has looked like for Pennsylvania agriculture,” said
Senator Judy Schwank
. “Every single one of us depends on our farmers and our agriculture sector provide us with the foods and products we need to go about our daily lives. Hearing from farmers and our Secretary Redding about Pennsylvania’s agricultural landscape is always valuable.”
“As someone who grew up farming, supporting the farmers and ag businesses I represent in Lancaster is a top priority for me,” said
Senator James Andrew Malone
. “Today, we heard from a farm operator in my district, Duane Swanger, that the rising cost of fuel, fertilizer, and seed are some of the biggest challenges our farmers are facing right now. We also heard that low-interest loan opportunities for farmers and support for addressing challenges like the avian influenza have been critical for his family’s farm. I look forward to continuing these critical programs and exploring new ways we can support farmers as they do the important work of feeding our state and nation.”
Secretary Russell Redding, Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture, testified on the state of the agricultural economy and its impact on our farmers and food system.
“Swirling around harvest and fall activities, every farmer is doing math right now, and this year the numbers are harder than they should be,” said Secretary Redding. “While no year is without challenges, the convergence of factors, such as climate disasters, rising prices on critical supplies such as diesel, geopolitical events, federal policy shifts, and market changes over the past several years have created a tremendously difficult farm economy, which has impacts on the foundations of our food system. But here is what farming has taught me: every time we plant a seed, we are making a bet on a strong harvest and a better tomorrow. In that spirit, today’s conversation is a seed – what we plant here, together, is how we make sure that tomorrow is better for Pennsylvania’s farmers, producers, and families who are counting on us.”
Noah Erwin, the Associate Director for Policy at Pasa Sustainable Agriculture, emphasized the need to help farmers maintain viable businesses and work environments.
“First, making important changes to our farmland preservation program would go a long way in helping to keep farmers farming,” said Erwin. “USDA’s 2022 Census of Agriculture showed that Pennsylvania leads the nation in the percentage of farmers under 35. We should be proud of that and continue to invest in programs that encourage young folks to farm. If we want to keep these folks in farming, however, we must do more to help make long-term land access and security a reality. Buying, or even leasing, land has become all but impossible in some places. An off-farm job for at least one, if not both, adults in the household is necessary to have the cash flow for affording land.”
Erwin also testified that Pennsylvania should also join the 16 other states who allow all workers to apply for a driver’s license.
“Currently, half of workers hired in agriculture do not have immigration status or work permits,” said Erwin. “Providing driver’s license access to all workers in agriculture and food sectors supports farm businesses and our food system and also makes our roads safer. House Bill 1518 is one of the proposals out there, though it has also not received a vote.”
Matt Espenshade, the President of the Pennsylvania State Grange and a seventh-generation dairy farmer from Lancaster County spoke on the future of agriculture.
“For our family, the future of agriculture is not an abstract policy discussion. It is the question of whether the next generation will have a fair opportunity to farm,” said Espenshade. “Pennsylvania agriculture supports more than 48,800 farms, contributes approximately $132.5 billion to the Commonwealth’s economy and supports nearly 600,000 jobs. Those numbers demonstrate agriculture’s strength, but they can hide how financially fragile many individual farms remain. Farmers face volatile commodity prices, severe weather, animal disease, workforce shortages and sharply higher costs for fertilizer, fuel, electricity, feed, equipment and repairs.”
In addition, Espenshade highlighted the impact of Chobani’s decision to invest $1.2 billion in a Pennsylvania facility, a move regarded as one of the most significant opportunities the dairy industry has seen in a generation.
“The project is expected to create more than 900 jobs and, at full scale, source more than three billion pounds of Pennsylvania milk each year – approximately 30 percent of the milk currently produced in the Commonwealth,” said Espenshade. “Production is expected to begin in 2027. That new demand is tremendously encouraging, but milk production cannot be expanded with the flip of a switch. Growing a herd requires cows, feed, land, barns, manure storage, financing, permits and trained workers. Farmers will need dependable market signals and sufficient time to make responsible decisions. Public policy should help farms grow carefully and profitably, not pressure them into expansion without secure contracts or sound business plans.”
Testifiers for the hearing included:
Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture
Pasa Sustainable Agriculture
Penn Ag Industries
Pennsylvania State Grange Office
Duane Swanger, Farm owner and operator from Conoy Township
Senator Nick Miller was elected Policy Chair of the Senate Democratic Caucus in December 2024.

title: Pennsylvania Senators, Advocates, Rally in Harrisburg for Access to Contraceptives
raw_text:
Pennsylvania Senators, Advocates, Rally in Harrisburg for Access to Contraceptives
September 28, 2026
Harrisburg, PA − September 28, 2026 –
This morning,
Senator Amanda M. Cappelletti
(D-17, Montgomery/Delaware),
Senator Maria Collett
(D-12, Montgomery), and
Senator Judy Schwank
(D-11, Berks), rallied with First Lady Lori Shapiro, Pennsylvania House colleagues, national experts, and Planned Parenthood advocates to
call for action on
Senate Bill 1112
.
The legislation would require all insurers to provide coverage for contraceptives, eliminate most co-payments for related coverage, remove pre-authorization requirements for certain contraceptives, and authorize insurers to cover up to 12 months of birth control at one time.
“The reproductive healthcare landscape right now is a scary place for Americans,”
said Senator Cappelletti, Co-Chair of the Pennsylvania Women’s Health Caucus.
“The federal government has made it clear they are willing to go to extreme lengths to threaten our access to care. Pennsylvania must respond to show our communities we will protect their health and wellbeing when other officials in Washington are too busy buying into conspiracy theories.”
Following the
Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization
Supreme Court ruling
, nationwide threats to family planning clinics have increased. Prior to
Dobbs
,
publicly funded family planning clinics provided contraceptive care to one quarter of all U.S. women receiving such care
. Many of these clinics have been forced to close their doors, or struggle to operate as the Trump administration withholds
Title X
and
Medicaid
funding. The Republican Federal Spending Bill—H.R. 1—passed in 2025 has
posed additional threats to Medicaid
, which covers FDA-approved contraceptives for people in all 50 states.
“Americans across the political spectrum agree that people should be able to access contraception and decide for themselves whether and when to start or grow a family,” said
Dana Singiser, co-founder of the Contraceptive Access Initiative
. “At a moment when misinformation about contraception is increasingly driving the national debate, it has never been more important that people have accurate information, real access to the methods that are right for them, insurance coverage for over-the-counter contraception and clarity about their rights. I’m grateful to Pennsylvania’s leaders for shining a light on an issue that matters to families across the Commonwealth and the country.”
Contraceptives offer a variety of uses. While they are commonly used to prevent unintended pregnancies, forms of contraceptives serve a number of medical purposes, often including hormone regulation, family planning, and treatment for severe conditions like endometriosis, dysmenorrhea, and Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (previously known as PCOS).
“While out-of-touch rightwing politicians continue to threaten our essential healthcare freedoms, we gathered today to share a clear message: we will not back down in our fight to protect and expand Pennsylvanians’ access to contraceptives,”
said Senator Maria Collett.
“Our colleagues in the House have taken action. The question now is whether or not Senate Republicans have the courage and the common sense to stand with the majority of Pennsylvanians who agree that birth control access should not be a partisan issue.”
The Pennsylvania House of Representatives has already taken steps to protect access to contraceptives.
Representative Mary Jo Daley (D-168, Montgomery)
has introduced
House Bill 2605
, which would prohibit the Commonwealth from interfering with the use of medically appropriate methods of contraception or fertility treatments. In May 2025, the House also voted 116-87 in support of Representative Leanne Krueger’s (D-161, Delaware)
House Bill 1140
, companion legislation to SB 1112.
“House Democrats have been working hard to champion contraceptive access for all Pennsylvanians by passing bills that protect our right to full reproductive healthcare. This includes HB1140, which has passed the House two sessions in a row with bipartisan support, but the Senate has failed to move the bill,”
said Representative Leanne Krueger.
“With a federal government that is openly hostile to reproductive rights, we must enshrine protections in state law to ensure access to contraceptives, safeguard privacy, and remove barriers to essential reproductive health tools. This is the time for action.”
House Bill 1140 has been stalled in the Senate Banking and Insurance committee since June 3, 2025. The committee is chaired by Republican Senator Chris Gebhard.
“All women in this Commonwealth should have access to full reproductive healthcare, and that includes access to contraception,” s
aid Representative Gina H. Curry, (D-164, Delaware), who co-sponsored House Bill 1140 and serves a co-chair of the Pennsylvania Women’s Health Caucus.
“This is about agency—the power to make decisions about our own bodies, our families and our futures. Women deserve the freedom to determine if and when motherhood is part of their journey and to have access to the healthcare that makes that choice real. When cost, geography or other systemic barriers stand in the way, they limit not only healthcare, but opportunity. Reproductive equity means removing those barriers so every woman has the power and resources to determine the course of her own life and family.”
Governor Josh Shapiro has continued to fight for Pennsylvanians to have access to the full spectrum of reproductive healthcare, and polling shows
strong bipartisan support for increasing access to contraception.
After decisive action in the House, Senate Democrats, advocates, and partners are calling on the Senate Republican majority to finally send these bills to the Governor’s desk.
“Access to quality health care is something every woman deserves, but we know that in some communities access to health care can be a real challenge, especially for women in rural communities,”
said First Lady Lori Shapiro.
“Contraceptives play an essential role in women’s health care and making sure they are accessible is just plain common sense.”
“A lack of access to contraception affects every Pennsylvanian, whether we realize it or not. We have an opportunity to follow the example set in the House of Representatives and advance legislation that protects access to essential reproductive health care,”
said Senator Schwank.
“Ensuring that all Pennsylvanians can obtain the contraception they need to live healthy lives is good policy and the right thing to do.”

He has also served as a member of Shillington Borough Council, the Governor Mifflin School Board, and numerous nonprofit and professional organizations.

Lawmakers and Advocates Call for Enactment of Legislation to Protect Manufactured Home Communities
June 9, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA — June 9, 2026 —
Pennsylvania lawmakers joined advocates and manufactured home residents today to voice support for legislation that would protect homeowners from steep land-lot rent increases.
Across the country, manufactured home communities are increasingly being purchased by private equity firms, hedge funds and multi-state corporations that then dramatically raise rates. Manufactured homeowners own their homes, but not the land beneath them, and relocating a manufactured home is often costly and difficult.
As a result, homeowners living in communities purchased by private equity firms have little recourse when rates sharply increase. Many manufactured homeowners are seniors, veterans and people with disabilities who live on fixed incomes and are increasingly at risk of being priced out of their homes.
Legislation has been introduced in the Pennsylvania General Assembly to significantly strengthen protections for residents of manufactured home communities. Proposed provisions include requiring 180 days’ notice of all rent and fee increases, capping annual increases based on the Consumer Price Index (with justified exceptions and temporary capital improvement surcharges), and granting residents and resident associations a 90-day right of first refusal when parks are put up for sale.
HB 1250
, introduced by Rep. Liz Hanbidge (D-Montgomery), passed the Pennsylvania House of Representatives on June 10, 2025, by a vote of 144-59. Senate Urban Affairs & Housing Committee passed
SB 746
, introduced by Sen. Judy Schwank (D-Berks), which gives manufactured home residents the right of first refusal, on June 8, 2026 unanimously.
Gov. Josh Shapiro
called on the Legislature
earlier this year to pass bills to protect manufactured homeowners and included the reforms in his 2026-27 budget proposal. Participants at Tuesday’s press conference expressed urgency to get the legislation enacted before the end of the current session.
“The clock is ticking, and further delay isn’t an option,” said Schwank. “These are commonsense reforms that will protect hardworking Pennsylvanians and help keep them in their homes. It’s critical that we stand with these homeowners and enact this legislation before the session ends, so we don’t have to start this entire process over again in 2027.”
“It was an honor today to support the residents of manufactured home communities as they fight to protect themselves from out of state bad actors,” said
Senate Democratic Leader Jay Costa
. “I look forward to championing the legislation put forward by Senator Schwank to empower Pennsylvanians who call these communities home. Let’s get this done.”
“Manufactured housing is one of the last pathways to affordable homeownership in Pennsylvania,” said Hanbidge. “HB 1250 provides reasonable protections against excessive and unjustified rent hikes. It creates fairness, predictability, and stability while still allowing community owners to operate successfully. That’s why Democrats and Republicans in the House came together to pass it. Because housing affordability should never be a partisan issue.”

Senate Approves Schwank’s Resolution to Study Municipal Planning Code
April 22, 2026
Reading, PA — April 22, 2026 —
The Pennsylvania Senate yesterday passed
Senate Resolution 211
, introduced by Sen. Judy Schwank (D-Berks), which directs the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee to conduct a comprehensive study of the
Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code
.
Pennsylvania’s Municipalities Planning Code was enacted in 1968 and serves as the framework for governing land use planning, zoning, subdivision, and development decisions for municipalities and counties. The study conducted by the LBFC, a bipartisan, bicameral legislative service agency, is tasked with evaluating how the code is performing and recommending improvements.
“Pennsylvania’s communities have changed considerably in the nearly 60 years since we established the land use law that our communities are still relying on,” said Schwank. “This study will give us an honest, independent look at how the code is performing and where the commonwealth can do better in supporting municipalities as they plan for growth, housing, and economic development. We need to modernize our municipal planning code to meet today’s challenges.”
The Berks County Planning Commission worked with Schwank on this effort and supported the resolution. Ashley Showers, the Executive Director of the Berks County Planning Commission, stressed the need to make improvements to the planning code.
“The approval of Senate Resolution 211 marks a pivotal opportunity to modernize the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code,” said Showers. “The Planning Commission looks forward to this comprehensive review and the insight it will bring, as its findings will directly influence our daily work—guiding how we support municipalities, review development proposals, and implement effective, forward-looking planning practices that better serve our communities.”
The final vote in the Pennsylvania Senate was 46-2.

State Sen. Judy Schwank (D-Berks) and City of Reading Mayor Eddie Moran applauded a $700,000 award through the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency’s Community Revitalization Fund Program to support the redevelopment of 418 and 422 Penn St. in downtown Reading.
The total cost of the Aston Investment Group-led project is $6.5 million. The development will transform two long-vacant historic buildings into a mixed-use anchor along Penn Street, the city’s main commercial corridor.
Upon completion, the project will deliver 12 workforce housing units on the upper floors of the rehabilitated structures. The development will also include approximately 25,000 square feet of flexible commercial space across 11 suites designed to accommodate a range of uses, including professional services, retail, cafes, personal care providers and creative studios.
Schwank called the award a welcome sign of continued progress for Reading’s downtown corridor.
“We all understand the value in improving our downtown,” Schwank said. “Supporting the folks who see opportunities in the City of Reading and helping them succeed using the tools we have at our disposal at the state and local levels is critical.”

“This is a great win for the City of Reading and another strong step forward for our downtown,” Moran said. “Projects like this help bring long-vacant buildings back to life, add needed housing, and strengthen Penn Street as a commercial corridor. We’re thankful to PHFA for this investment, and to Sen. Schwank for her continued support and advocacy for Reading. I also want to recognize our grants team and our Downtown Manager for the work they put in to help make this happen and keep our downtown moving in the right direction.”
The developer behind the project, Aston Investment Group, called the funding critical to bringing the Penn Street vision to life.
“On behalf of Aston Investment Group, we are honored to be awarded $700,000 in grant funding from the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency.
